title: Windows 11 Clean Install
steps: Back up your files — a clean install wipes the drive.
Download the Windows 11 ISO from Microsoft and create a bootable USB with Rufus (8 GB or larger).
Enter firmware setup and confirm UEFI mode with Secure Boot enabled and TPM 2.0 active.
Boot from the USB, choose language, and click Install now.
Enter your product key or choose 'I don't have a product key' to activate later.
Select Custom install, delete old partitions on the target drive, and install to unallocated space.
Complete the out-of-box experience: region, keyboard, network, and Microsoft account.
Run Windows Update repeatedly until no updates remain, then install drivers from your PC maker's site.
commands:
diskpart
list disk
select disk 0
clean
convert gpt
exit
description: A clean install of Windows 11 starts with a bootable USB made from Microsoft's official ISO and requires UEFI firmware with Secure Boot and TPM 2.0. Booting the USB and choosing Custom install lets you wipe the drive and lay down a fresh copy. After the out-of-box experience, Windows Update and manufacturer drivers finish the job.

list disk
select disk 0
clean
convert gpt
exit

title: Bootable USB with dd
steps: Identify the USB device with lsblk — triple-check it is not your system disk.
Unmount any mounted partitions on the USB.
Run dd with a 4 MB block size and oflag=sync for a clean write.
Wait for dd to finish (use status=progress to watch it).
Run sync, then eject the device.
Boot the target PC from the USB via the boot menu key.
commands:
lsblk -d -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL
sudo umount /dev/sdX1 2>/dev/null || true
sudo dd if=~/ubuntu-24.04-desktop-amd64.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress oflag=sync
sync
description: The dd command writes an ISO byte-for-byte to a USB device on Linux and macOS — no special tool needed. The critical step is identifying the right /dev/sdX device, because dd overwrites whatever you point it at without asking. status=progress shows the copy in real time.

title: GPT vs MBR Partitioning Schemes
steps: Learn the limits: MBR supports 4 primary partitions and 2 TB disks; GPT supports 128 partitions and huge disks.
For any PC made after ~2012 with UEFI firmware, choose GPT.
Use MBR only for legacy BIOS systems or old tools that demand it.
In Windows setup, diskpart 'convert gpt' switches an empty disk to GPT.
In Linux, gdisk creates GPT tables; fdisk handles MBR.
Converting a disk with data destroys it — back up first.
Match the scheme to the firmware mode: UEFI boots GPT, legacy BIOS boots MBR.
commands:
diskpart
list disk
select disk 0
clean
convert gpt
create partition efi size=512
format fs=fat32 quick
assign letter=S
description: GPT is the modern partition table: 128 partitions, disks far beyond 2 TB, and checksums that detect corruption. MBR is the legacy 1980s scheme limited to four primary partitions and 2 TB. UEFI firmware expects GPT; mixing UEFI with MBR is the most common cause of 'no bootable device' errors.

demo.program:
diskpart
list disk
select disk 0
clean
convert gpt
create partition efi size=512
format fs=fat32 quick
assign letter=S

title: UEFI vs Legacy BIOS Boot
steps: Enter firmware setup (Del, F2, or F12 at power-on, varies by maker).
Find the Boot section and check whether UEFI or Legacy/CSM mode is active.
For Windows 11 and modern Linux, use UEFI mode with CSM disabled.
Disable CSM/Legacy to force pure UEFI booting and avoid mixed-mode installs.
Ensure the boot order lists your USB or SSD before other devices.
Save and exit; the installer must boot in the same mode as the target install.
Verify in Windows with msinfo32 (BIOS Mode: UEFI) or in Linux via /sys/firmware/efi.
commands: ls /sys/firmware/efi/efivars && echo 'Booted in UEFI mode' || echo 'Booted in Legacy BIOS mode'
description: UEFI replaced legacy BIOS with a modern firmware interface supporting GPT disks, Secure Boot, and faster startup. Installing an OS in one mode while the firmware uses the other produces an unbootable system. Checking /sys/firmware/efi on Linux or msinfo32 on Windows confirms which mode you booted.

title: Secure Boot Setup
steps: Enter firmware setup and find the Secure Boot option under Security or Boot.
Set Secure Boot to Enabled and the mode to Standard (not Custom) for Windows.
For Linux, use a distribution with a signed shim: Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian all qualify.
If Linux refuses to boot, check that the distro's shim is signed — unsigned kernels are blocked.
Custom mode lets you enroll your own keys (MOK) for self-compiled kernels.
Dual-boot setups work fine as long as each OS boots through signed loaders.
Leave Secure Boot on unless a specific driver or OS requires it off.
commands:
mokutil --sb-state
sudo mokutil --import mykey.der   # enroll a Machine Owner Key (custom mode)
description: Secure Boot is a UEFI feature that only runs bootloaders signed with trusted keys, blocking bootkits and rootkits. Windows requires it, and major Linux distributions ship a Microsoft-signed shim so they boot with it enabled. Custom kernels need your own Machine Owner Key enrolled via mokutil.

title: Dual-Boot Windows and Ubuntu
steps: Install Windows first — it overwrites bootloaders, so it must go first.
In Windows, shrink the C: partition from Disk Management to free space for Ubuntu.

Boot the Ubuntu USB in UEFI mode and choose 'Install alongside Windows'.
Let Ubuntu use the freed space, or partition manually for control.
Finish install and reboot — GRUB now offers both Windows and Ubuntu.
If Windows boots straight through, check UEFI boot order puts ubuntu first.

powercfg /h off
# In Ubuntu, if GRUB missed Windows:
sudo update-grub
sudo os-prober

Ubuntu's installer detects Windows and adds it to the GRUB boot menu automatically. Shrinking Windows from inside Windows keeps its filesystem safe before Ubuntu claims the freed space.

title: Dual-Boot with Separate Drives
steps: Install each OS on its own physical drive for maximum isolation.
Disconnect the other drive during each OS install to protect its bootloader.
Install Windows on drive 1 with the Linux drive unplugged.
Install Linux on drive 2 with the Windows drive unplugged.
Reconnect both drives; set the Linux drive first in UEFI boot order.
Run sudo update-grub so GRUB detects Windows on the other drive.
Select the OS at the GRUB menu each boot, or change the default in /etc/default/grub.
commands:
sudo os-prober
sudo update-grub
sudo grub-install /dev/sda
description: Putting each OS on its own drive is the most robust dual-boot: neither installer can touch the other's bootloader. Unplugging the idle drive during each install removes all risk of picking the wrong disk. GRUB on the Linux drive then chainloads Windows, giving one menu for both.

title: LVM Setup During Install
steps: Understand LVM: physical volumes hold volume groups, which hold resizable logical volumes.

sudo resize2fs /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv

title: LUKS Full-Disk Encryption
steps: Back up everything — enabling LUKS on an existing system wipes the disk.
In the Ubuntu/Fedora installer, tick 'Encrypt the new installation' or set up LUKS manually.
Choose a strong passphrase: 20+ characters, unique, stored in a password manager.
The installer creates a LUKS container holding LVM volumes inside.
At every boot you enter the passphrase to unlock the disk.
Add a keyfile on a USB for unattended servers, kept physically secure.
Test reboot twice before trusting the setup — a lost passphrase means lost data.

sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sda2 cryptroot
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/mapper/cryptroot
description: LUKS is Linux's standard disk encryption: the entire partition is encrypted and unlocked at boot with your passphrase. Installers for Ubuntu, Fedora, and Debian offer one-checkbox LUKS setup. There is no recovery backdoor — losing the passphrase permanently destroys access to the data.

t: Swap Partition and Swap File Setup
title: Swap Partition and Swap File Setup
steps: Decide: a swap file is flexible and the modern default; a partition suits hibernation.
To make a 4 GB swap file: fallocate, chmod 600, mkswap, swapon.
Add the swap file to /etc/fstab so it survives reboots.
For hibernation, the swap partition must be at least as large as RAM.
Check with free -h and swapon --show; tune swappiness in /etc/sysctl.conf.
On installers, 2-4 GB of swap covers most desktops; servers size to workload.
Remove swap cleanly with swapoff before deleting the file or partition.
commands:
sudo fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
description: Swap gives Linux overflow room when RAM fills and enables hibernation to disk. Modern installers default to a swap file, which can be created, resized, or removed without repartitioning. A 4 GB swap file covers typical desktops; swappiness tuning controls how eagerly the kernel uses it.

sudo fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

title: GRUB Repair and Reinstall
steps: Boot from a live Ubuntu USB and connect to the internet.
Identify your Linux root partition with lsblk -f.
Mount root at /mnt and bind-mount /dev, /proc, /sys, plus the EFI partition.
chroot into /mnt and reinstall GRUB to the disk (not a partition).
Run update-grub to rebuild the boot menu and detect other OSes.
For UEFI, ensure grub-efi is installed and the EFI partition is mounted at /boot/efi.
Reboot without the USB; GRUB should present the menu again.
commands:
sudo mount /dev/sda2 /mnt
sudo mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/boot/efi
for d in dev proc sys; do sudo mount --bind /$d /mnt/$d; done
sudo chroot /mnt
grub-install /dev/sda
update-grub
exit
description: GRUB breaks most often when Windows reinstalls its own bootloader over it. Repair means booting a live USB, mounting the installed system, chrooting in, and running grub-install plus update-grub. UEFI systems need the EFI partition mounted at /boot/efi during the repair.

title: PXE Network Install Basics
steps: Set up a server on the LAN with DHCP, TFTP, and HTTP services.
Install dnsmasq for combined DHCP+TFTP or ISC DHCP plus tftpd-hpa.
Place the netboot files (pxelinux.0 or iPXE) in the TFTP root.
Serve the OS installer files over HTTP/NFS from the same server.
Configure the DHCP server to point clients at the TFTP boot file.
Enable network boot in each client's firmware and boot — the installer loads over LAN.
Automate with preseed/kickstart files for hands-free installs.

# enable-tftp
# tftp-root=/srv/tftp
